indicators.note: the crosses come after, so behind, the letter for old

parts.note: X is the shape of a cross
to ford a river is to cross it, so crosses can be read as the verb fords, giving FORD

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about angry people at the back of a historic English town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crosses' does double duty as two pieces: the letter X, which looks like a cross, and FORD, a verb for crossing water.
explanation.definitionFit: The university town on the Thames is a well-known English city.

clue.text: Spend too much where in France, admitting something to do with money, ultimately

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: French for where is ou
a verb is a doing word

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone asks where in France they might splurge on something financial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'something to do' is a schoolroom definition of a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To overbuy is to purchase more than needed, so to overspend.

indicators.note: short means cut, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a rib is a bone
sotto is the Italian word for under

explanation.surface: A recipe note: a small bone goes beneath an Italian dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under Italian' looks like a position, but it asks for the Italian word for under, SOTTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Risotto is a creamy rice dish from Italy, a classic main course.

clue.text: Tree where laid-back snake bitten by half-cut monkey

indicators.note: something bitten is gripped inside the jaws, so one piece sits inside the other
cut in half, the monkey loses its second three letters

parts.note: a baboon is a large monkey

indicators.note: laid back means turned to face the other way, so the snake is read backwards

parts.note: a boa is a constricting snake

explanation.surface: A jungle scene: a relaxed snake is bitten by a tipsy monkey beside a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, which suits the surface; here it means chopping the monkey's name in half. 'laid-back' sends the snake backwards before it is bitten.
explanation.definitionFit: The baobab is an African tree with a famously swollen trunk.

parts.note: praise, long and runs are verbs, and a mock grammar lesson would say what ... and number they are in

explanation.surface: A review saying a playwright's work earned acclaim and lengthy seasons.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is AYCKBOURN. The clue reads as praise for a hit play, but asks for the grammatical label of verbs such as 'runs', made silly: one of his best-known comedies.
explanation.definitionFit: Absurd Person Singular is a 1972 Ayckbourn comedy, and its title plays on the grammar term for a verb's form.

clue.text: Bovine to eat etc, mashed with one fork

indicators.note: something eaten is taken inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a bison is a bovine animal

indicators.note: mashed things are crushed into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A cow sits down to a meal of mashed food with a fork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fork' looks like cutlery for the bovine's meal, but it is the definition: a fork is a split in two. 'mashed' jumbles the etc, and 'to eat' puts that inside the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A fork is where something splits in two, which is a division into two parts.

parts.note: a ... is a mess or travesty, so the word ... made into a ... of its letters gives boredom

explanation.walkthrough: 13 is AYCKBOURN, author of the 1975 comedy Bedroom Farce: rearrange the letters of BEDROOM and you get 'boredom'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedroom Farce is a 1975 stage comedy by Alan Ayckbourn, so it is one of his works.

clue.text: Warm bottom among three rated wobbly

indicators.note: among means in the midst of, so one piece goes inside
wobbly means unsteady, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the bottom of something is its end

explanation.surface: Something rated three stars has a wobbly, warm base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warm' is the definition in its sense of kindly; 'wobbly' jumbles the two words three rated, and 'among' sets the bottom in among them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tender-hearted person is kind and affectionate, i.e. warm in nature.

indicators.note: less means minus, so letters are taken out

parts.note: something improved is better

explanation.surface: A drinker claims a pint gets better once you stop abstaining.
explanation.walkthrough: TT, short for teetotal, comes out of BETTER to leave the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer is a common alcoholic beverage brewed from malt and hops.

clue.text: Socialist leader, despite amazing success initially, unfortunately resigns

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
things gone unfortunately have gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled
initially points to the first letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: A Socialist party leader quits despite a remarkable record of success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'despite' reads as a link in the surface but is anagram fodder; 'unfortunately' jumbles it together with the first letters of 'amazing success'.
explanation.definitionFit: To step aside is an idiom for giving up a post, the same as quitting it.

parts.note: the words 'primate' and 'principal' appear with their final words for a pal missing, so companions are not there

explanation.surface: A garbled note from a playwright's world, with words chopped off midway.
explanation.walkthrough: PRIMATE has lost MATE and PRINCIPAL has lost PAL: both chums are gone. 13 is AYCKBOURN, and this is the title of one of his plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Absent Friends is a 1974 comedy by Alan Ayckbourn, and the title also describes mates and pals who are missing.

clue.text: Writer taking you back in play — that's service!

indicators.note: letters put in play are moved around, so they are rearranged

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy, the senior British armed service

explanation.surface: A tennis writer takes you back to a match, praising a serve.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tennis serve, but the service is the Royal Navy, Britain's senior armed service. 'in play' jumbles the two words before it; 'taking' and 'that's' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Ayckbourn is a prolific English playwright, so a writer of stage comedies.

indicators.note: in a down entry, the bird sits on top of the other piece

parts.note: the knot is a wading bird
to shop someone is British slang for informing on them, as is to grass

explanation.surface: Someone describes a store with a bird perched above it, then names a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shop' and 'grass' are both British slang for telling the police about someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Knotgrass is a common straggling weed of fields and wasteland.

clue.text: Howard, perhaps, mild — if eccentric — cleric

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: a rector is a parish clergyman

explanation.surface: A vicar named Howard is described as gentle, if a little odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Howard' is not a vicar's name but Ron Howard, the American who directed Apollo 13; 'eccentric' jumbles mild if.
explanation.definitionFit: Ron Howard is an example of someone who directs movies, signalled by 'perhaps'.

definitions.meaning: a fruit ... is a creamy dessert, a British pudding
a sucker is a gullible dupe

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a whipped fruit pudding and someone easily tricked.

clue.text: Familiar bore, oddly kind and personal

parts.note: a bore is a drilled hole, such as a well

indicators.note: oddly takes the first and third letters of the word

parts.note: your own things are your personal ones

explanation.surface: A dull person turns out, strangely, to be warm and personal with you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' looks like a dull person but is a drilled shaft, a WELL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something widely recognised is famous or familiar to many people.

clue.text: Heading for aggro between supporters, one succeeds

indicators.note: between puts one piece in the middle of the others

parts.note: a leg supports a table or chair
a tee supports a golf ball

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Trouble breaks out among football fans as one side wins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supporters' supplies two pieces, one for furniture and one for golf; 'aggro' is British slang for violent trouble, apt for football supporters in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A legatee receives a legacy, so they succeed to someone's property.

parts.note: the word reads as BRA SHE IN, which is SHE inside BRAIN

explanation.walkthrough: 13 is AYCKBOURN. Split 'Brashein' as BRA(SHE)IN: SHE, a woman, sits in BRAIN, the mind, giving his 1985 play Woman in Mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Woman in Mind is a 1985 Ayckbourn play about a woman's breakdown, so one of his works.

definitions.meaning: a warm zip-up jacket worn on the upper body
to shaft someone is slang for cheating them

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a soft outer jacket and to swindle or rip off.

clue.text: Second corner knocked over ending in space, head back

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up upside down, so the two pieces read backwards

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
to hog something is to corner it for oneself

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Instructions for a manoeuvre in a game: take a corner, then retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked over' turns MOHOG into GOHOM; E, the end of 'space', completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: To go home is to return to where you live, i.e. to make your way back.

clue.text: Rotten thing, swimmer's heart not in dip

indicators.note: not in means left out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: hummus is a chickpea dip

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A swimmer refuses to go into the water, and something has gone bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dip' looks like a swim but is the chickpea paste; M, the centre of 'swimmer', drops out.
explanation.definitionFit: Humus is decayed plant and animal matter in soil, so rotted material.

clue.text: Act of containing people not starting with Roger

indicators.note: a word not starting loses its first letter

parts.note: men are people
Roger Casement was an Irish nationalist hanged for treason in 1916

explanation.surface: Someone notes that people refused to begin work alongside a man called Roger.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Roger Casement was a British diplomat turned Irish nationalist, executed in 1916; 'with' is a link joining the trimmed people to his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Encasement is the noun for enclosing something in a case or covering.

parts.note: to suss something is informal for working it out
ex means former, or old

explanation.surface: A puzzle about working out an old split between East and West.
explanation.walkthrough: SUSSEX is an English county split into East Sussex and West Sussex, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The county on England's south coast is divided administratively into East and West halves.
